account: On 2 January 2015 the Southern Nevada Health District (SNHD) began a controlled experiment with nEmesis, a University of Rochester system. It applies a support-vector-machine language model to geotagged tweets to rank Las Vegas food venues by foodborne-illness risk. During the first three months environmental health specialists inspected 142 venues, half chosen by nEmesis, half under the standard protocol. Inspectors were blind to which was which. Adaptive inspections uncovered 9 demerits per inspection versus 6 (p = 0.019). They found 11 venues graded C or worse versus 7 for controls, a 64% improvement. The abstract summarizes this as 63% more effective. Side findings included an unpermitted seafood establishment and a food handler working with an influenza-like illness. The authors estimate, from CDC outbreak averages, that adaptive inspections saved 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations over the three months. They estimate all of Las Vegas's 35,000+ annual inspections made adaptive could prevent over 9,126 cases and 557 hospitalizations a year. SNHD performed 5 foodborne-illness investigations between 2 January and 31 March 2015, against 11 in the same window the year before.

ai_role.statement: The AI chose which venues to inspect. The comparison was a controlled double-blind design with 142 venues split between nEmesis and standard protocol. So the difference in findings is attributable to the AI's venue selection. The developers (Rochester) are distinct from the deployer (SNHD), though SNHD staff co-authored the paper. The paper was peer-reviewed as an IAAI deployed paper.

fields.account: On 2 January 2015 the Southern Nevada Health District (SNHD) began a controlled experiment with nEmesis, a University of Rochester system. It applies a support-vector-machine language model to geotagged tweets to rank Las Vegas food venues by foodborne-illness risk. During the first three months environmental health specialists inspected 142 venues, half chosen by nEmesis, half under the standard protocol. Inspectors were blind to which was which. Adaptive inspections uncovered 9 demerits per inspection versus 6 (p = 0.019). They found 11 venues graded C or worse versus 7 for controls, a 64% improvement. The abstract summarizes this as 63% more effective. Side findings included an unpermitted seafood establishment and a food handler working with an influenza-like illness. The authors estimate, from CDC outbreak averages, that adaptive inspections saved 71 infections and 4.4 hospitalizations over the three months. They estimate all of Las Vegas's 35,000+ annual inspections made adaptive could prevent over 9,126 cases and 557 hospitalizations a year. SNHD performed 5 foodborne-illness investigations between 2 January and 31 March 2015, against 11 in the same window the year before.

display.answer: The system probably favored venues whose customers posted location-linked accounts of illness, so restaurants serving less visible social-media users were less likely to receive an algorithmic priority.
display.editor_note: The ranking depended on geotagged tweets rather than a population-wide sample of diners. Unequal posting therefore provides a direct mechanism for unequal visibility, although its size was not measured.

provenance.basis: Account: tweets ranked venues. replication: dense geotagged posting and enough flagged venues were necessary.
